results.content: Indeed, a growing number of higher education staff, faculty, and students have access to, and experience with, an ever-expanding array of AI-based tools and capabilities to support their work. It is essential, then, that staff, faculty, and students be trained to vet and thoughtfully adopt the bring-your-own-AI (BYOAI) tools that are not directly provided or supported by the technology team at their institution. Whether by choice or not, faculty in particular seem to be on the front lines of AI adoption at their institutions, navigating their own uses of these technologies while also supporting students' uses of them. Wake Forest University has taken a proactive and open-minded approach to encouraging staff, faculty, and students to experiment with AI across a range of use cases inside and outside the classroom. results.title: 7 AI Decisions That Will Define Higher Education In 2026 - Forbes
results.content: It’s what becomes the new operating model for teaching, assessment, student support, and workforce pathways in an AI-native world. Federal guidance has made clear that institutions may use grant dollars for AI in instruction, student support, and workforce programs, but only with civil-rights and privacy compliance—and with humans remaining accountable for high-stakes decisions. In 2026, the differentiator will be whether institutions can produce a living evidence trail: who owns AI decisions, what uses are permitted, how risk is assessed, how people are trained, how tools are monitored for drift and bias, and how policy evolves over time. In practical terms, the strategic play is to rebuild the pipeline: Make AI literacy universal across majors, require workplace AI experience through internships and co-ops, remake career services into skills-based advising, build stackable credentials tied to verified job data, and invest in AI-driven student success infrastructure that supports retention and equitable access to opportunity.
